name: picohttpparser AVX2 patch (Cloudflare / vkrasnov)
workload: bench.c and the fukamachi/fast-http benchmark (fukamachi.c) parsing HTTP requests, counting parses/operations per second, comparing the stock PCMPESTRI token-scan path to a new AVX2 bitmap-scan path
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.9.2, -mavx2 -mbmi2 -O3 (both versions built the same way)
hardware: Haswell Intel Core i5-4278U, turbo disabled
stars_or_usage: 20 stars (demo fork); AVX2 idea folded into Cloudflare's own HTTP stack
tradeoffs: AVX2-only (no runtime fallback in this patch), and the blog notes the naive latency-bound port of PCMPESTRI to AVX2 was NOT faster - the win only came from restructuring the scan to be throughput-oriented (128-byte bitmap scan with TZCNT), which is a real algorithmic change, not just a wider instruction swap.
caveats: This is a demo/PR-linked fork, not merged upstream into h2o/picohttpparser at HEAD; numbers are from a single 2014-era Haswell laptop CPU and a 2014 compiler. README confirms dual MIT/Perl license inherited from upstream picohttpparser but GitHub detects no SPDX license file in the fork itself.

name: Picozig (zig-pico)
workload: Parsing HTTP request lines/headers in a tight loop via `zig run -O ReleaseFast src/request/bench.zig`, reported as requests-per-second and headers-per-second
claimed_speedup: >5,000,000 req/s for Picozig (without SSE4) vs ~3,200,000 headers/s claimed for original picohttpparser (without SSE4) - roughly 1.6x, README's own framing
compiler_and_flags: zig run -O ReleaseFast (Zig version not stated)
hardware: AMD 8845H mobile CPU (for the Picozig side only; the picohttpparser figure is not stated to have been measured on the same machine)
tradeoffs: Partial translation of picohttpparser to pure Zig; explicitly does not implement chunked transfer-encoding; no SSE4/SIMD path at all, so the comparison is scalar-vs-scalar; single-file, unaudited, no test suite visible in README.
caveats: The picohttpparser baseline number (~3.2M headers/sec) is quoted from memory/elsewhere in the README, not re-measured on the same AMD 8845H hardware as the Picozig number, so this is not an apples-to-apples same-machine comparison - treat the 1.6x-ish ratio as approximate. No license file; zero stars; single contributor.

name: jianrong7/http-parser (Go zero-alloc parser)
workload: Go benchmarks (testing.B, go test -bench) parsing a simple GET (2 headers), a POST with JSON body, and a GET with 8 headers, measuring ns/op, allocations, and MB/s
claimed_speedup: ~10x faster on simple GET (133ns vs 1,377ns) and POST+body (161ns vs 1,602ns), ~5x faster on GET with 8 headers (374ns vs 2,021ns); 0 B/op vs 5,177-5,345 B/op allocations; 495-641 MB/s vs 48-98 MB/s throughput
tradeoffs: In-place, zero-copy parsing into caller-owned byte slices - offsets are only valid while the buffer is unmodified; README lists explicit 'What's Missing' gaps versus net/http's full feature set (e.g. no chunked-body reassembly convenience, no cookie jar/multipart helpers mentioned).
caveats: Benchmark code (parser/parser_test.go) is public in the repo and hardware is stated, but Go compiler version/GOFLAGS are not stated, so this falls short of Tier A; net/http is not one of the three named baselines for this category (llhttp/http-parser/picohttpparser) but is the de facto incumbent for Go HTTP parsing, so baseline_in_list=false. Zero stars, very new/unreviewed.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search repos "http parsing" fast -> jianrong7/http-parser README

name: FasterAPI HTTP/1.1 parser
workload: Unspecified micro-benchmark of the HTTP/1.1 request-line/header parse path, reported as a single per-call nanosecond figure
claimed_speedup: 12ns per parse, described as '40x faster than llhttp API'
tradeoffs: Author states the parser's state machine was itself imported/adapted from llhttp's generated tables rather than being an independent design; project is explicitly framed as an experimental testbed, not a production library.
caveats: No workload, hardware, compiler, or flags are stated anywhere in the doc; the '40x' figure compares calling the imported llhttp state machine directly versus going through llhttp's full public API, which is not a like-for-like comparison of two independent parsers (it likely mostly measures API/wrapper overhead, not parsing-algorithm speed). Treat as a weak, unverified first-party claim. Repo docs folder is literally named 'archive' and the file 'ULTIMATE_ACHIEVEMENT.md', consistent with unreviewed self-marketing copy.
found_via: Blogs / talks: gh search code "than llhttp" -> Ugbot/FasterAPI docs/archive/ULTIMATE_ACHIEVEMENT.md
